posts.c: In 2026, our photo editors chose Gabriel Jensen’s (@shallowseasgallery) image of a banded jawfish as our Your Shot Photo of the Year. These fish are known as mouth brooders because they protect their fertilized eggs by holding them in their mouths until they’re ready to hatch. Jensen hovered motionless above over the fish’s burrow in the shallow waters of Florida’s Lake Worth Lagoon for almost an hour to get this shot, using a dim red light to illuminate the fish while trying not to spook it. Is that car floating? 🤔 Your brain can see movement in a completely still image, even when absolutely nothing is moving. Optical illusions exploit the way your brain processes colors, contrast, shadows, and patterns. Some illusions, such as the rotating snakes illusion, can make stationary circles appear to spin because of how your visual system responds to changes in brightness. Surprisingly, your brain doesn’t simply record what your eyes see. It constantly interprets visual information and makes predictions about the world. This explains why two identical lines can appear different lengths, why stationary images seem to move, and why people can perceive the same picture differently. Like this content? posts.c: The earliest known physician in recorded history lived more than 4,600 years ago, long before modern medicine existed. Imhotep, an ancient Egyptian who lived around 2600 BCE, is often credited as one of history’s earliest known physicians. However, evidence of his actual medical practice is limited. He was also an architect and high-ranking official who helped design Egypt’s famous Step Pyramid of Djoser. Surprisingly, Imhotep became so respected that Egyptians eventually worshipped him as a god of medicine and healing. Centuries later, the Greek physician Hippocrates, often called the Father of Medicine, helped establish the idea that diseases had natural causes rather than being punishments from the gods. His name remains associated with the Hippocratic Oath, a symbol of medical ethics today. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: Like if you get them 🤣 Onions make you cry because they release a chemical that turns into a mild acid when it touches the moisture in your eyes. When you cut an onion, damaged cells release enzymes that produce a gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. This irritates your eyes, triggering tears to wash it away. Surprisingly, chilling onions before cutting them can reduce the amount of irritating gas released. Even more surprisingly, onions have been cultivated for over 5,000 years and were so important in ancient Egypt that they were placed in tombs. Their circular layers symbolized eternity, and archaeologists have found onions associated with Egyptian burial rituals. Onions also contain sulfur compounds that contribute to their distinctive smell and flavor. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

Three high voltage pylons stand in the saturated brine of a working salt pond near Newark, on San Francisco Bay, California. The brine is coloured red by microorganisms that thrive in hypersaline water. The darker patterns under the surface are old marsh channels, where the tide once flowed in and out. Around 85% of the bay’s tidal wetlands were lost over the last century and a half, but about 15,000 acres of former salt ponds nearby are now being restored to tidal marsh. What draws me to places like this is that the industrial landscape still carries the outline of the natural one underneath. I photographed it in August 2025, handheld from the open window of a small plane."" - Alex Visbal (@alexvisbal) Alex Visbal won our Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category in #WPY62 for his powerful documentation of how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland. This week offers is a time to slow down, reconnect with friends and family, make a few memories, put a bird on it, and maybe spend some time outdoors. Whether it’s a walk in the woods, a visit to a favorite park, or simply enjoying the company of those around you, there’s a lot to be thankful for. Like leftovers. Speaking of food, did you know birds and bison have a mutually beneficial relationship? True story. Birds often hitch ride on a bison in search a good meal. Also, a good taxi in a pinch, though it’s rather stop and go. As bison graze and move through tall grass, they stir up insects that birds can easily catch, while some birds also pick ticks and other parasites from the bison’s hides. It’s a pretty great partnership. Sharing is caring! One animal’s leftovers become another’s feast, and everyone leaves the table (back of a bison) happy. NPS Photos

I used to get confused by the different types of holiday cacti, and honestly, I don’t blame anyone who does. They look pretty similar until you know what to look for... So I decided to draw out the leaf structures (technically stems!) of the three main types to make them easier to tell apart. The Thanksgiving cactus (Schlumbergera truncata) has those distinctive hooked, claw-like edges. It’s actually the one you’ll most commonly find at nurseries, even though it’s often mislabeled as a Christmas cactus. The actual Christmas cactus (Schlumbergera bridgesii) has smaller, smoother edges. Kind of funny that it’s one of the harder ones to find, considering how often we hear the name. Then there’s the Easter cactus (Rhipsalidopsis gaertnerii), which has smoother edges with a little bristly look to them. Of course, you’ll still run into plenty of variations. posts.c: One of the most famous cartoon tropes, characters running off cliffs without falling until they look down, is based on a deliberate violation of physics! Popularized by Looney Tunes, this gag is part of a set of unofficial animation principles often called cartoon physics. Characters can survive explosions, flatten themselves like pancakes, and recover from injuries that would be fatal in real life. Surprisingly, many cartoon tropes originated from practical animation techniques. Characters often wear the same clothes because consistent designs make them easier to animate, while exaggerated facial expressions help communicate emotions instantly. These conventions became so recognizable that audiences understand them without explanation, even when they make absolutely no logical sense. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: If you’re looking for a simple seafood recommendation this mahi-ght be the one! Buy: ✅ Mahi mahi caught by U.S. fisheries Avoid: 🛑 Imported mahi mahi Mahi are large pelagic fish that mature quickly and have lots of offspring! That makes them less susceptible to overfishing. The main environmental sustainability concerns come from how they’re caught. Fishers use longlines and purse seines to capture these flashy fish, but these methods can have a lot of bycatch if not properly managed. Sticking with U.S.-caught mahi is a good way to ensure your fish comes from strictly regulated fisheries that take measures to reduce bycatch. 🐬Dolphinitely a better choice for the sea! #SeafoodWatch #SustainableSeafood #MahiMahi #Dolphinfish #USCaughtSeafood

Would you cut your own Christmas tree in the Green Mountain National Forest? For just $5? It’s one of our favorite holiday traditions! For just $5 per tree (plus a $2.50 online service fee on recreation.gov), you can get a permit, head into the woods, and bring home your very own wild Christmas tree. We’ve been doing this for 20 years, and every year is a little different. Sometimes we find a beauty. Sometimes we bring home a Charlie Brown tree. But it’s always so much fun! A few things to know before you go: 🌲 Permits are $5 per tree, with a limit of two per household. 🌲 Trees must be 20 feet tall or less. 🌲 You can only cut in designated areas of the National Forest. 🌲 Bring a saw, rope, a tarp (or sled), and a little patience. 🌲 Bringing your pups is part of the fun. You can purchase your permit online through Recreation.gov. Be sure to download the harvest map and check the rules before heading out. Last year, work started with flagging and removing introduced invasive plants. This fall, staff and volunteers planted superstar native plants like black cherry, serviceberry, and dogwood in their place. As these plants grow, they’ll help improve water quality and provide critical habitat for birds, turtles, and other wildlife.

For a few hours this summer, streets across Vermont were transformed. The streets that normally divide our neighborhoods with fast traffic suddenly became filled with people. When we close our streets to traffic for a block party, people can safely drag their whole lives out onto the road. They play games and music, eat potluck dinners, chat and meet their neighbors, maybe for the very first time. The most painful part of a block party is announcing that it’s over. Kids drag their feet in the middle of their games, adults cut their conversations short, and the cars start flowing through again. What if it didn’t have to end? Read Jack Evan's full report, Streets Should Be Places, at the link in our bio.

All a teen needs is a laptop, tablet or smartphone; a desire to gain new skills; and the motivation to take a project — such as a website, app, circuit board or gaming console — from concept to completion. The goal isn’t to make things to sell but to learn and share freely with others. posts.c: Onions have layers. Stars have layers. Webb’s mid-infrared instrument is giving us new details on supernova remnant Cas A, helping astronomers chronicle the structure and evolution of Cas A’s original star. Stars form as gravity causes clouds of dust and gas to collapse, ultimately triggering the internal fusing of hydrogen into helium. Mechanisms within the star cause it to fuse heavier and heavier elements and as this process repeats, a star can develop shells of these elements. When high mass stars end their lives dramatically in a supernova explosion, the elements created within the star get spread into space, ultimately allowing new stars to form. Webb (guided by data from the retired Spitzer Space Telescope - slide 2) found evidence that shortly before the supernova explosion, the shells of elements created in the star merge, causing the layers to mix, changing the structure of the star, and thus the chemical composition of its remains. Do bears hibernate? Kind of. (That’s a scientific term.) Hear us out. Bears actually enter a state called torpor. Their metabolism slows, their body temperature drops, and they can go for long periods without eating, drinking, or doing much of anything. Essentially, they’ve mastered the art of doing absolutely nothing. It’s a gift. Unlike true hibernators, bears can wake up relatively easily and may even become active during warmer spells. Does that mean they’re leaving the den for happy hour every night? Not quite. But they might stretch their legs, take a little loop around the neighborhood, doom scroll online, or just check whether anything interesting has happened while they’ve been asleep. Flight delays? Email down? And back to the den. NPS Images

Have you ever wondered how a forest changes over its lifetime? Last week, we introduced you to early-successional forests. As these young forests grow back from a disturbance, they enter their version of the teenaged phase. While they still support some plants and animals, they lack the structural complexity of their younger and more mature counterparts. These forests are no longer young, with abundant and dense trees and shrubs up to 20 ft in height. They also have not reached an older, more mature condition, with multiple layers of vegetation, small gaps in the canopy overhead, large diameter standing dead trees, and large logs on the forest floor. Thoughtful stewardship can help introduce the habitat diversity needed to sustain more biodiverse and resilient forest communities. Get started fostering biodiversity in your forest. Two stars enter... Webb observed the aftermath of a star merger, helping astronomers piece together the fate of the pair. Stellar mergers are very hard to predict, and thus hard to observe. But in 2023, astronomers noticed an unusual variable star that had a consistent brightness in 2018. By September 2024, the object, nicknamed “Bao,” was starting to brighten and also spew dust. Bao faded in visible light but brightened in infrared in July 2025. When ground-based telescopes caught an eruption on October 17, 2025, multiple telescopes swung into action. posts.c: There’s no practical reason to grow your own wheat. Buying flour is cheaper in every way… But I grow it anyway. This year I planted out a 3x35' plot. The last time I grew it my yield was pretty mediocre...but I still baked 3-4 sourdough loaves that tasted absolutely amazing Growing the wheat is less than half the job tho - at harvest time you cut it, thresh it (knock the grain loose from the stalks), winnow it (toss it in moving air so the light chaff blows away and the heavy grain falls), and then mill it into flour 3 months of growing + that entire post-processing saga yielded me ~10 pounds of homegrown wheat this summer. More than enough to make a FULLY homegrown banana bread with my own bananas, my own flour, and eggs from the backyard hens Outside of growing my own vanilla and sugarcane, that’s about as close as I’m gonna get to a fully homegrown baked good. Is it practical? Absolutely not. But is it fun? Hell yeah

posts.c: Rho, Rho, Rho your Oph...🎶 Rho Ophiuchi is a striking star-forming cloud, filled with gas and stars of different sizes and ages. Chandra reveals infant stars that violently flare and produce X-rays. Infrared data from Webb provides views of the cloud’s regions of gas and dust. When this data is made audible, through a process known as data sonification, Chandra’s X-rays become high-pitched glassy tones, along with other sustained sounds to mark the appearance of extended bright sources. The clouds in Webb’s infrared data are mapped as differently pitched sounds, and stars are played as metallic plucks. There is a gap in the middle of the piece due to dark dust clouds that emit very little light. #Space #Universe #Sonification #Astronomy #Stars

Before European colonization, this time of year is when landlocked Atlantic salmon would swim into the tributaries of Vermont’s large lakes to spawn. Now, as we work to keep populations of these prized fish healthy and ultimately to restore them in their native waters, November is the time when we gather salmon eggs to rear in our hatcheries around the state. Pictured here, staff at our Bald Hill Fish Culture Station collect salmon eggs from hatchery-dwelling broodstock to supplement the eggs harvested from feral fish in Vermont's bigger waters of Lake Champlain, Lake Memphremagog, Lake Willoughby and Seymour Lake.

A bighorn sheep's face when someone says, "Nice antlers!" *bighorn sheep sigh* 😑 So, what's the difference between antlers and horns, anyway? Horns are a two-part structure. An interior portion of bone (which is an extension of the skull) is covered by an exterior sheath grown by specialized hair follicles (similar to human fingernails). Horns are usually found on both males and females of pronghorn, bison, and bighorn sheep. Antlers grow as an extension of the animal's skull. They are true bone, a single structure, and generally found only on males of the deer family. Antlers are also shed and re-grown each year, while horns are usually never shed and continue to grow throughout an animal's life. One exception to this rule is the pronghorn, which sheds and re-grows its horn sheath each year. Photo (NPS / Jacob W. Frank): 1. Bighorn sheep ram with large, curved horns. 2. Bull elk with large antlers. 3. Pronghorn buck with horns.

Burying food scraps in your garden sounds like an easy way to feed your plants, but there’s a little more soil science involved than you might think. Organic matter doesn’t become plant food overnight. Soil microbes, fungi, and other decomposers have to break it down first, converting complex organic compounds into simpler nutrients that plant roots can eventually absorb. Here’s the catch: decomposition takes time, and fresh organic materials can temporarily tie up nutrients as microbes consume them to do their work. Depending on the material, its carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and how quickly it breaks down, burying food scraps can actually delay nutrient availability rather than give plants an immediate boost. Materials like raw animal tissue also need time to decompose, which can make nutrient release unpredictable. Asparagus is a perennial because it has an underground storage system that keeps it coming back year after year. The crown, a cluster of buds and roots just below the soil, stores carbohydrates that fuel new spear growth every spring. Its deep, established root system also helps the plant access water and nutrients beyond the reach of many shallow-rooted vegetables. Here’s the interesting part: those feathery ferns aren’t just extra foliage. They’re the plant’s solar panels. Through photosynthesis, they capture sunlight and convert it into sugars, which are transported down to the crown and stored as energy reserves. The more energy the crown accumulates during the growing season, the more resources it has to produce healthy spears in the seasons ahead. That’s why harvesting asparagus too early can set the plant back. Every spear you cut is a potential fern that could have been producing energy for the underground crown. Letting those spears mature allows the plant to build the reserve

posts.c: Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar invites the young and young at heart to connect with ocean life through movement and play. The ocean moves us! Hold on like a seahorse—there are plenty of them here and so much more to discover! Just swipe left and sea. African penguins are back in a newly expanded habitat! Watch as they groom and dive off the rocks. Then, practice your penguin waddle in this new interactive space. A 20-foot-long coral reef includes giant clams and a bluespotted ribbontail ray that glides along the sand. Nearby, clownfish nestle into anemones. Enjoy multiple play areas that are welcoming to visitors of all ages. There’s also plenty of rest areas to relax and check out the ocean views of Monterey Bay! Watch leaping blennies hop across wet stones! Visitors can also follow shapes in the floor to hop from rock to rock like blennies. posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👇 Cars use several types of filters to protect their engines, improve performance, and keep passengers comfortable. Air filters prevent dust and dirt from entering the engine, oil filters remove contaminants from engine oil, and fuel filters stop impurities from reaching the fuel system. These filters help reduce wear, improve efficiency, and extend the lifespan of important components. Cabin air filters also clean the air entering the passenger compartment, trapping dust, pollen, and other airborne particles. Interestingly, a clogged filter can reduce engine performance, restrict airflow, or cause unpleasant smells inside the car, depending on which filter is affected. Regular filter replacement is one of the simplest ways to keep a vehicle running smoothly.

posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! We are so appreciative of all the outpouring of love that we’ve seen from our community and wanted to share an update on what was found after a necropsy was performed on Fiona. The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible. No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked. The other hippos, Bibi, Tucker, and Fritz, are eating and behaving normally. It’s difficult to know how they’re feeling, but they appear to be their normal selves. Keepers, vets, staff, and volunteers are shaken and trying to navigate this loss. She meant a lot to a lot of people.

It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency. The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week. Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover. We know everyone in the community will be crushed by this news, as we all are. Please keep her keepers and everyone who tried to help her in your thoughts as they try to navigate and come to terms with this shocking news. They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time.
